# Writing a heartfelt thank-you speech for a community award with Qwen Chat

**Hook:** By the end of this guide you'll have a draft thank-you speech that sounds like you — not a robot — ready to print, practise, and deliver. This is for anyone who has just been recognised at a community event, an awards night, a school function, or a volunteer gathering, and isn't sure where to start.

## Before you start
- A free **Qwen Chat** account. Sign up at chat.qwen.ai with an email address — no credit card is needed for the basic free plan.
- A modern web browser on a computer, tablet, or phone. The free plan is usually enough for a short speech; paid tiers may give longer replies and fewer waiting periods.
- A few minutes to think about **who** you're thanking and **why** this moment matters to you.
- Total time: roughly **20–30 minutes**, including a couple of rounds of edits.

One honest note before we start: Qwen Chat is brilliant at drafting words on a page, but it cannot stand on stage and deliver the speech for you, and it does not know your life. The real magic happens when you feed it your own memories — then it shapes them into sentences you actually want to say.

## Step 1 — Open Qwen Chat and start a fresh conversation
Open your browser and go to **chat.qwen.ai**. After signing in (or creating a free account if you haven't yet), you'll see a chat page with a large text box near the bottom and a sidebar on the left. Look for a button labelled "New Chat" or a small "+" icon to begin a fresh conversation, and click it. **What happens next:** a blank chat thread opens, ready for your first message. **If it looks different:** on some devices the new-chat option may be hidden under a menu icon (three dots or three lines) — tap that and you'll find "New Chat" inside. **You'll know it worked when** you see an empty conversation area with the text input box empty and ready for you to type.

## Step 2 — Tell Qwen the basics about the award and your audience
In that text box, type a short paragraph explaining the situation: what award you received, who's in the room, and roughly how long you want to speak. A "prompt" is just the instruction you give to an AI — think of it as the brief you'd hand to a writer friend. Press Enter or tap Send. **What happens next:** Qwen usually replies within a few seconds, either asking a clarifying question or offering a first draft. **If it looks different:** if the reply feels generic, don't worry — that's normal on the first message. Just add a bit more detail and send it again. **You'll know it worked when** Qwen responds with something that acknowledges your specific award and your specific audience.

💬 Example: *I just received the "Volunteer of the Year" award from our local community centre. Around 60 people will be at the ceremony — mostly neighbours I've worked with for years, plus my family. I'd like a 2-minute thank-you speech (about 300 words) that feels warm and genuine, not formal or stiff.*

## Step 3 — Ask for an outline before asking for a full draft
Before Qwen writes the whole speech, ask it to draft a short outline first — usually four to six bullet points. This is a small but powerful habit: it lets you reshape the structure before any words are locked in. Type your request and send. **What happens next:** Qwen produces a list of suggested sections, often something like an opening thanks, a personal story, gratitude to specific people, and a closing thought. **If it looks different:** if Qwen jumps straight to a full speech instead, simply reply with "Can you give me a short bullet-point outline first?" and it will adjust. **You'll know it worked when** you have a list of sections that roughly matches the journey you want to take your listeners on.

💬 Example: *Great start — before you write the full speech, can you give me a 5-point outline I can review first? Keep each point to one sentence so I can reshuffle them.*

## Step 4 — Feed in your real stories and specific names
This is where the speech starts becoming yours. Tell Qwen one or two genuine memories — the names of people who helped you, a moment that surprised you, something funny or moving that happened. The more concrete you are, the warmer the draft will feel. Type these into the chat and ask Qwen to rewrite the relevant section using them. **What happens next:** Qwen produces a revised version that weaves your details into the structure from Step 3. **If it looks different:** if the new version still sounds too formal, ask it to "make it sound more like I'm talking to a friend over a cup of tea". **You'll know it worked when** the draft contains a real name or moment that only you could have supplied.

💬 Example: *Please rewrite the "gratitude" section using this: when I first started volunteering I was terrified of public speaking, and a woman named Margaret quietly coached me through my first committee meeting. We're still friends eight years later. She couldn't be at the ceremony tonight and I'd like to mention her by name.*

## Step 5 — Refine the length and tone until it sounds like you
Read the draft out loud — yes, really, because your ear catches what your eyes miss. Ask Qwen to shorten or lengthen it, soften the tone, or replace any sentence that doesn't feel right. Think of this step as a back-and-forth conversation with a writing assistant. **What happens next:** Qwen produces a cleaner version with each round of edits. **If it looks different:** if a response feels repetitive, simply say "Try again, but make every sentence different" and it'll rewrite fresh. **You'll know it worked when** you can read the whole speech out loud without cringing, and it ends naturally inside your time limit.

💬 Example: *Please cut this down to about 350 words and make it sound warm and conversational — like I'm genuinely thanking people, not reading a report. Keep the Margaret story near the end and make it the emotional heart of the speech.*

## Common mistakes
- **Skipping your own stories.** The draft will sound generic if Qwen only has the basic facts. Fix: spend five minutes listing two or three real moments before you start — names, places, small incidents that come to mind.
- **Accepting the first draft.** The first response is rarely the best one. Fix: treat the output like clay — keep reshaping and re-prompting until it sounds like you, not like an AI.
- **Forgetting to read it aloud.** A speech that reads well on paper can feel awkward when spoken. Fix: read it out loud once. If you stumble over a sentence, that sentence needs reworking.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same back-and-forth technique works for any personal writing — birthday messages, retirement tributes, eulogies, or wedding toasts where you want warmth without the stress.
- **For your business or work:** you can use the exact same steps to draft a short acceptance speech for a workplace award, an industry panel thank-you, or a community-board acknowledgement at a public meeting.
- **If you're just getting started:** open Qwen Chat, paste in the 💬 example from Step 2, and see what comes back. That's the whole entry point — no planning needed, and you can edit from there.

## Try it now
Open chat.qwen.ai, start a new chat, and paste this in: *I just received a community award I'd like to thank people for at a small ceremony. Help me write a short, warm thank-you speech of about 250 words. Ask me three questions first so the speech actually sounds like me.* Whatever Qwen replies with is your starting point — and from there you're only a few edits away from something you can be proud to say out loud.
